title: Debugging as a method
tagline: A repeatable loop for going from 'it is broken' to the line, config, or row that broke it, without guessing.
why: Banging your head on a bug usually means guessing: changing things that feel likely and hoping. A method replaces that with cheap experiments, each of which rules out half of what is left. This day is the core skill the rest of the course feeds, and the one you will use every week.
objectives: Write a problem statement with expected behavior, actual behavior, scope, and start time, and ask what changed
Choose between reproducing first and reading code first, and between logging, a debugger, and a failing test
Bisect a failure over commits, layers, config, data, or time, and estimate how many steps it will take
Read a chained Python traceback bottom up and separate the root cause from the error that reached the top
Recognize when a fix made an error disappear without explaining it

lessons.title: The loop: observe, hypothesize, test, narrow

blocks.text: Debugging is running experiments. You hold a set of possible causes, run the cheapest test that rules out a large part of that set, and repeat until one cause is left that explains every observation. Guessing skips the middle step: it applies fixes and waits to see whether the symptom goes away.

blocks.title: The debugging loop

steps.label: State expected vs actual, precisely
steps.detail: What should happen, what happens instead, for whom, since when, how often.
steps.fail: A vague statement such as 'chat is broken' makes every theory look plausible.

steps.label: Ask what changed
steps.detail: Deploys, config, dependencies, data, traffic, upstream providers, and the clock.
steps.fail: Skipping this sends you into the code when the cause is a config edit at 14:02.

steps.label: List hypotheses and rank them
steps.detail: Rank by likelihood and by how cheap each is to test. A cheap test of a medium suspect often comes first.
steps.fail: Holding only one hypothesis turns every result into confirmation.

steps.label: Predict, then test one thing
steps.detail: Write what you expect to see if the hypothesis is true, then change or measure exactly one thing.
steps.fail: Changing three settings at once leaves you unable to say which one mattered.

steps.label: Record the result and what it rules out
steps.detail: A timestamped line per experiment: what you did, what you saw, what is now excluded.
steps.fail: Without notes you retest the same idea an hour later, or hand over nothing.

steps.label: Narrow and repeat until one cause explains all
steps.detail: Stop only when the cause accounts for every observation, including when it started and who it affects.
steps.fail: Stopping when the symptom vanishes leaves the cause in place.

blocks.title: A debugging notebook, first fifteen minutes
blocks.code:
14:20 STATEMENT  Expected: POST /chat returns a reply. Actual: 500 for ~8% of
                 requests since 14:05. Text-only tickets fine. Staging fine.
14:22 CHANGED?   Deploy v2.14 at 13:40. Config: none. Provider status: green.
14:24 H1 deploy  H2 one bad pod  H3 specific ticket data  H4 upstream LLM
14:26 TEST       500s by pod: spread evenly over all 6 pods.   -> H2 out
14:29 TEST       500s by tool called: all inside lookup_order. -> H4 unlikely
14:31 TEST       500s by ticket: all have attachments.         -> H3 up
14:33 NOTE       v2.14 went out 25 min before the first 500. Check timing again.
notes: The statement names scope (8 percent, attachments) and a start time. Both are evidence.
Each test is a grouping of data you already have. None changes production.
The deploy is the first suspect, but the 25-minute gap does not fit a deploy that affects every request. The notebook keeps that doubt visible.

blocks.caption: Two ways to run the same experiment
rows: 'If the pool is exhausted, errors stop at pool size 40'
One hypothesis gains, the others lose
A hypothesis is ruled out and recorded
Often a query over existing logs
blocks.verdict: Prefer experiments that read existing evidence over ones that change the system. Grouping failures by pod, version, tenant, or input costs minutes and often halves the search.

blocks.title: What changed? Check these first
blocks.text: Code deploys, config and feature flags, dependency versions, the data (a new customer, a new order format, a table that crossed a size), traffic shape, upstream providers, and the clock (certificate expiry, month-end, daylight saving time). Most production bugs start at a change.

blocks.title: The change that happened nearby is not always the cause
blocks.text: A deploy shortly before an incident is the most tempting suspect and is often right. It is wrong when the timing does not quite fit, or when the failures are limited to inputs the deploy did not touch. Check the timing to the minute and the scope before you blame it.

blocks.title: Customers are failing and a recent deploy is suspect

options.name: Roll back
gain: Fastest way to stop the damage
Tests the deploy hypothesis as a side effect
cost: Loses the new features for a while
Unsafe if a migration or data change cannot be undone
options.choose: Choose this when the deploy plausibly caused it, rollback is safe, and you do not yet know the fix.

options.name: Fix forward
gain: Keeps the rest of the release
No risk from reversing a migration
cost: Customers keep failing while you write and ship the fix
A rushed fix can add a second bug
options.choose: Choose this when the cause is understood, the fix is small, or rolling back is unsafe.

blocks.title: What changed, for an LLM system
blocks.text: Add the model version, the prompt, the tool schemas, the retrieval index, and the eval dataset to the list. Outputs vary from run to run, so a single rerun is not a test: run the case several times and compare rates.

blocks.q: Relay's 500s started at 14:05. A deploy went out at 13:40, and every 500 involves a ticket with an attachment. What should you check before rolling back?
options: Whether the deploy changed anything about attachments
Whether Postgres CPU is high
Whether the LLM provider is degraded
blocks.explain: The scope says attachments, and the timing leaves a 25-minute gap. If the deploy never touched attachment handling, something else changed at 14:05, such as a new attachment type arriving. One look at the diff splits the two.

blocks.text: A **reproduction** is a way to make the failure happen on demand. With one, each experiment takes seconds. Without one, each experiment waits for production to fail again. Most of the time spent on a hard bug is spent getting a reliable reproduction, and then the fix is quick.

blocks.title: Where to start on a new bug

options.name: Reproduce first
gain: Every later test is fast and certain
You can confirm the fix by watching the failure stop
cost: Capturing inputs and environment takes time
Some failures depend on production load or data
options.choose: Choose this for most bugs, and always before claiming a fix.

options.name: Read the code first
gain: Fast when the traceback points at an obvious line
Works when a reproduction is impossible
cost: Code shows what should happen, not what did
Easy to find a plausible bug that is not this bug
options.choose: Choose this when the evidence already points at a few lines, then confirm with a reproduction.

items: The exact request: body, headers, user, ticket, and time.
The versions: commit, image tag, dependency lockfile.
The effective config: environment variables and flags as the process saw them, not as the file says.
For an LLM call, the full request: system prompt, messages, tools, model, temperature.
The data the request touched: the order, the ticket, the retrieved chunks.

blocks.text: Reduce it to the smallest failing case

A **minimal reproduction** is the smallest input and setup that still fails. Remove half of what is left; if it still fails, keep the cut, otherwise put it back and try the other half. A 40-message conversation that breaks the agent usually shrinks to one message and one tool result, and the cause is then easy to see.

blocks.caption: Why it works locally and fails in production
rows: A flag on in production, off locally
Print effective config in both and diff
A row with an unusual format or size
Replay the exact production input locally
A library a minor version apart
Diff installed versions, not just the lockfile
A proxy, a timeout, TLS in between
Check which identity the process runs as
blocks.verdict: Do not guess which difference matters. Make the local setup more like production one difference at a time until it fails, and the last change you made is the cause.

blocks.title: Works locally, fails in production
blocks.text: First replay the exact failing input locally. If it now fails, the cause is the data, and you have a reproduction. If it still passes, the cause is the environment: diff effective config and installed versions next, since those are cheap, before suspecting concurrency.
Intermittent failures

A bug that fails one time in fifty is not random. Something differs between the failing run and the others: a race between two requests, a particular input, one bad instance, a timeout under load, or randomness in the code or the model. Your job is to find the attribute that separates failures from successes, and to raise the failure rate so each test gives an answer.

blocks.title: 400 replays of a failing chat request, grouped
blocks.code:
condition                         runs   failures
sequential, one at a time          200          0
two messages, same ticket, <50ms   100         31
two messages, different tickets    100          0

failures by worker:   w1: 8   w2: 7   w3: 9   w4: 7
failure text (all 31): duplicate key value violates unique
                       constraint "messages_ticket_id_seq_key"
notes: The rate went from about 2 percent in production to 31 percent under one condition. That condition is the clue.
Failures spread evenly over workers, so a single bad instance is ruled out.
Only concurrent messages on the **same** ticket fail. That points at a race on per-ticket state.

blocks.title: How to look inside the failure

options.name: Add logging
gain: Works in production and on rare failures
Leaves a record for next time
cost: Each round needs a deploy or a restart
Too much logging buries the signal
options.choose: Choose this when the bug only happens in production or too rarely to catch live.

options.name: Attach a debugger
gain: See every variable at the moment of failure
cost: Needs a local or reproducible failure
Pausing changes timing and can hide races
options.choose: Choose this when you can reproduce locally and the question is what the state looks like.

options.name: Write a failing test
gain: Stays as a guard against the bug returning
cost: Hard for failures that need real load or services
options.choose: Choose this as soon as you can reproduce, before writing the fix.

blocks.title: Reproducing an LLM failure
blocks.text: Store the full request that produced a bad answer, then replay it 20 times and count how often it fails. Temperature 0 reduces variation but does not guarantee identical outputs. A failure rate is a usable reproduction, and a fix should move it to near zero.

blocks.q: A tool call fails one time in fifty in production. Replaying the same request 200 times locally never fails. What is the best next move?
options: Conclude the bug is fixed in the current code
Replay with production-like concurrency and compare failure rates
Add a retry around the tool call
blocks.explain: The local run removed something production has. Concurrency is a common missing ingredient, and adding it back while measuring the rate tests that difference directly. A retry hides the failure without explaining it.

blocks.text: **Bisection** is binary search applied to a bug. When you have a known good state and a known bad state, test the midpoint. Whichever half the midpoint falls in, the other half is cleared. Each test halves what is left, so 1,000 suspects take about 10 tests, while checking them in order of suspicion can take hundreds.

blocks.caption: Things you can bisect
rows: Last release that worked, current head
Build the middle commit and run the reproduction
Call the middle hop directly, such as FastAPI behind nginx
Apply half of production's differing settings to staging
Check the error rate at 12:00 in metrics
Old prompt passes the eval, new one fails
Apply half of the edits and rerun
blocks.verdict: Bisect whenever you can name a good state and a bad state and test any point between them. The hard part is a reliable test, not the search.

blocks.title: Bisecting a refund failure over 75 commits
blocks.code:
$ git bisect start
$ git bisect bad HEAD
$ git bisect good v2.13
Bisecting: 37 revisions left to test after this (roughly 5 steps)
$ git bisect run ./scripts/repro_refund.sh
running './scripts/repro_refund.sh'
...
running './scripts/repro_refund.sh'
a91c3e7 is the first bad commit
commit a91c3e7
    Parse refund amounts with Decimal instead of float
$ git bisect reset
notes: `v2.13` is the last state known to work. Without a trusted good end, bisection has nothing to search between.
`git bisect run` uses the script's exit code: zero marks a commit good, most non-zero codes mark it bad.
The result is the commit where behavior changed. That commit may have exposed an older bug rather than written a new one, so read it before blaming its author.

blocks.title: Bisecting with a flaky test
blocks.text: If the reproduction fails one time in five, a bad commit can pass and be marked good, and bisection confidently names an innocent commit. Make the test reliable first, or run it several times per step and mark a commit good only if every run passes.
Bisecting the request path

blocks.title: Relay's request path, and the midpoint test at each layer

layers.name: Browser
layers.role: Sends the request and shows the result.
layers.breaks: Console errors and failed network calls show what the browser saw, but not why.

layers.name: Load balancer
layers.role: Terminates TLS and spreads traffic across nginx nodes.
layers.breaks: Its own logs show whether a request reached a backend and the status it got back.

layers.name: nginx
layers.breaks: Access and error logs show the upstream status and upstream time. A 502 with tiny upstream time means the app never answered.

layers.name: FastAPI
layers.role: Runs the handler and the agent loop.
layers.breaks: Calling it directly from inside the network splits the path: works directly means the fault is above it.

layers.name: Postgres and Redis
layers.role: Hold tickets, orders, cache, and counters.
layers.breaks: Running the handler's query by hand shows whether the data or the query is wrong.

layers.name: LLM API
layers.breaks: Replaying the logged request shows whether the model's output or your handling of it is wrong.

blocks.text: Start in the middle. If calling FastAPI directly fails the same way, the browser, load balancer, and nginx are cleared in one step. If it works, the fault is above it, and you test nginx next. The same move works on config: when staging and production differ in 40 settings, copy 20 of production's values into staging and see which half carries the bug.

blocks.title: Bisecting over time
blocks.text: When something broke but nobody knows when, use metrics to find the first bad minute. Narrow the window by halves on the error rate graph, then list every change in the minutes before it: deploys, config reloads, cron jobs, certificate renewals, provider incidents.

blocks.title: Bisecting an eval regression
blocks.text: A new prompt with six edits drops the pass rate. Apply three edits and rerun on the same dataset and model, then halve again. Each rerun must be large enough, or repeated enough, that the difference is bigger than run-to-run noise, or the bisection follows noise.

blocks.q: About 1,000 commits separate the last good release from the bad one. With a reliable reproduction script, roughly how many builds will bisection need?
options: About 10
About 100
About 500
blocks.explain: Each step halves the range, and 2 to the 10th is 1,024, so about 10 steps. Testing commits one by one in a guessed order could take hundreds, which is the whole case for bisecting.

blocks.prompt: A nightly batch job fails on one of 10,000 help-center articles, and the error does not say which. How would you find the article, and how many runs should it take?
blocks.answer: Split the articles in half and run each half. Keep the half that fails and split again. About 14 runs isolate one article out of 10,000, since 2 to the 14th is 16,384. Then fix the job's error message so it names the article next time.

lessons.title: Reading errors and stack traces, and the traps

blocks.text: An error message tells you where the program noticed a problem. That is often not where the problem began. A **stack trace** lists the chain of function calls active at that moment, and reading it well means finding the first place a wrong value appeared, then asking why it was wrong.

blocks.title: A chained traceback from Relay's agent
blocks.code:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/app/relay/tools/orders.py", line 38, in lookup_order
    order = await fetch_order(int(args["order_id"]))
ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'A-8812'

The above exception was the direct cause of the following exception:

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/app/relay/api/chat.py", line 88, in chat
    reply = await run_agent_turn(ticket, message)
  File "/app/relay/agent/loop.py", line 132, in run_agent_turn
    result = await call_tool(name, args)
  File "/app/relay/agent/tools.py", line 57, in call_tool
    raise ToolError(f"{name} failed") from exc
relay.agent.tools.ToolError: lookup_order failed
notes: 'Most recent call last' means the bottom frame of each block is where that exception was raised. Read each block from the bottom up.
The last line, `ToolError: lookup_order failed`, is what your error tracker shows. It describes the symptom.
'The above exception was the direct cause' means the code wrapped an earlier error with `raise ... from`. The first block is the original.
The root error is a `ValueError` on `'A-8812'`. The question to ask next is why an order id has a prefix, not how to stop `int()` from failing.

items: Read the last line: the exception type and message.
Look for chain markers and scroll to the first block, which holds the original error.
In that block, find the bottom frame in your own code, skipping library frames.
Note the values involved, from the message or from logs for that request id.
Ask where that value came from, and follow it upstream until it was last correct.

blocks.caption: How an earlier error shows up, or does not
rows: Raised a new error `from` the old one
'The above exception was the direct cause of the following exception'
A deliberate wrap; the first block is the original
'During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred'
The error handler itself failed; the first block is still the original
The cause was hidden on purpose; look in logs
Caught and returned a default, or logged only the message
No traceback, and a strange value later
The evidence is gone; the failure surfaces far away
blocks.verdict: When a traceback seems to start in the middle of nowhere, look for a swallowed or hidden cause upstream of it.

blocks.title: The error that points far from its cause
blocks.text: `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'status'` in the reply formatter usually means some earlier function returned `None` instead of failing. Search for the broad `except` that turned a real error into `None`, and make it log the full traceback or re-raise.
The traps

blocks.caption: Four ways a competent person gets stuck
rows: 'It must be the cache, and look, here is a cache miss'
Ask what you would see if your theory were false, and look for that
'I wrapped it in try/except and the error is gone'
Require an explanation for why it started, not just that it stopped
'It broke after the deploy, so revert my PR'
Check the timing to the minute and whether the deploy touches the failing path
'The log says the flag is off'
Check the timestamp, the host, and the environment of every line you rely on
blocks.verdict: All four feel like progress. The defense is the notebook: a written prediction for each test makes a wrong theory visible.

blocks.title: The fix made the error disappear without explaining it
blocks.text: Raising a timeout, adding a retry, or catching an exception can stop the error while the cause stays. Test your explanation: remove the fix, recreate the original condition, and watch the failure return. If you cannot say why it started when it did, you have not found it.

blocks.title: Agents hide tracebacks from you
blocks.text: When a tool raises, Relay returns the error text to the model as a tool result, and the model often apologizes or works around it. The final answer looks fine or vaguely wrong. Read the tool results in the trajectory, and log the full traceback on the server side.

blocks.q: Your error tracker groups a spike under `ToolError: lookup_order failed`. Where is the most useful information?
options: In the ToolError's own line, which names the failing tool
In the first traceback block of the chain, above the 'direct cause' line
In the FastAPI frame at the top of the second block
blocks.explain: The ToolError is a wrapper that names the symptom. The chain marker says an earlier exception caused it, and that first block holds the original type, message, and the line in your code where the bad value was used.

blocks.prompt: A teammate fixed the 'A-8812' traceback by stripping everything before the dash. Errors stopped. What question should you ask before accepting the fix?
blocks.answer: Is order 'A-8812' the same order as 8812? If the prefix marks a different sales channel, stripping it fetches the wrong customer's order and returns it confidently. The fix removed the error without explaining why ids changed format.

causes: Production data the local setup never sees
Different effective config or flags
Different installed dependency versions
Concurrency or a proxy only production has
fieldGuide.look: The exact failing production input replayed locally, then a diff of effective config and installed versions.
fieldGuide.confirm: The local run fails once you add the one production difference.
fieldGuide.fix: Fix that difference, and add the input or setting to tests so the gap stays closed.

fieldGuide.symptom: Fails one time in fifty, and a retry works
causes: A race between concurrent requests
One bad instance or node
A rare input
Timeouts under load or randomness
fieldGuide.look: Failures grouped by instance, input, concurrency, and time, compared with successes.
fieldGuide.confirm: Under one condition the failure rate jumps, for example to 30 percent with concurrent requests on the same record.
fieldGuide.fix: Fix the mechanism the condition reveals. A retry only hides it, and may repeat side effects.

fieldGuide.symptom: Error message points far from the cause, such as 'NoneType' has no attribute in unrelated code
causes: An earlier error swallowed and turned into None
A cause hidden with raise from None
fieldGuide.look: Where the None value was produced, and broad `except` blocks on that path.
fieldGuide.confirm: Logs for the same request id show an earlier exception, or the function returns None for a known bad input.
fieldGuide.fix: Let the original error propagate or log it with its traceback.

fieldGuide.symptom: The fix made the error disappear, but nobody can say why it started
causes: A retry, timeout bump, or exception handler masking the cause
fieldGuide.look: Whether the explanation accounts for when it started, who it affects, and how often.
fieldGuide.confirm: Removing the fix and recreating the original condition brings the failure back.
fieldGuide.fix: Keep the mitigation if it helps, but keep the investigation open until the cause is named.

fieldGuide.symptom: Errors started at a specific minute with no deploy
causes: Config or flag change
New kind of data arriving
Upstream provider change
Time-based event such as certificate expiry or a cron job
fieldGuide.look: The first bad minute in metrics, then every change log, cron schedule, and provider status in the minutes before it.
fieldGuide.confirm: One change lines up to the minute and explains the scope of the failures.
fieldGuide.fix: Revert or correct that change; add it to whatever change log you check first next time.

fieldGuide.symptom: Error tracker shows only a wrapper error such as ToolError, with no useful message
causes: The tracker groups by the last exception in a chain
The cause was raised from None or not logged
fieldGuide.look: The full event: the first traceback block above 'direct cause' or 'during handling'.
fieldGuide.confirm: The first block holds a specific error type and value.
fieldGuide.fix: Always chain with `from exc`, and include the identifying value in the wrapper's message.

fieldGuide.symptom: git bisect names a commit that cannot plausibly cause the bug
causes: A flaky reproduction marked a bad commit good
The wrong commit was chosen as the good end
fieldGuide.look: The bisect log, and how reliable the reproduction script is.
fieldGuide.confirm: Rerunning the script several times on the named commit's parent gives mixed results.
fieldGuide.fix: Make the reproduction reliable or repeat it per step, then bisect again.

fieldGuide.symptom: Cannot reproduce at all, with the same code
causes: Missing the exact input, user, or data
Missing the environment difference
fieldGuide.look: What the failing request carried and touched, from logs keyed by its request id.
fieldGuide.confirm: Replaying with the captured input fails.
fieldGuide.fix: Log enough per request to replay it: ids, inputs, versions, and for LLM calls the full request.

fieldGuide.symptom: The log says one thing and the system clearly does another
causes: Reading a stale log, the wrong host, or the wrong environment
Logs buffered and not yet flushed
fieldGuide.look: Timestamps, hostnames, and environment on the lines you rely on.
fieldGuide.confirm: The lines predate the incident or come from another environment.
fieldGuide.fix: Query logs by request id and time window, and include environment in every line.

glossary.def: A specific, testable guess at a cause, stated with the observation you would expect if it were true.
A way to make a failure happen on demand, so each experiment takes seconds instead of waiting for production.
The smallest input and setup that still fails, found by removing parts until any further removal makes it pass.
A failure that happens on some runs and not others. Something differs between failing and passing runs, and finding it is the work.
Binary search for a cause: test the midpoint between a good and a bad state, keep the half that contains the change, repeat.
A Git command that bisects over commits between a known good and a known bad one, optionally driven by a script's exit code.
The list of function calls active when an error was raised. In Python, the most recent call is printed last.
An exception raised while handling or because of an earlier one. Python prints the earlier one first, with a marker between them.
An exception caught and discarded or reduced to a message, so its traceback is lost and the failure appears later somewhere else.
The earliest fault that, if removed, prevents the failure. The error you see is usually a later consequence of it.
Noticing evidence that supports the theory you already hold and missing evidence against it.
Returning to the previous known good version to stop damage, before the cause is fully understood.

apply.title: Turn your last bug into a method
steps: Pick a bug from your project this month. Write one line each for expected, actual, scope, start time, and what changed. Notice which you did not know at the time.
Write a script that reproduces one current failure in your project and exits non-zero when it fails. Run it 20 times and record the failure rate.
Search your code for `except Exception` and bare `except`. For each one, check whether it logs the full traceback or re-raises, and fix one that does neither.
Find the last commit where your eval score or test suite was known good, count the commits since, and work out how many bisection steps it would take.

quiz.q: A service ran cleanly all morning. At 14:05 its error rate jumps from near zero to 8 percent. Which question is most likely to narrow the cause quickly?
options: Which function in the codebase is most likely buggy?
What changed in or around the system shortly before 14:05?
Would restarting the service make the errors stop?
Has the error rate been this high before?
quiz.explain: A sharp start at a known minute means something changed then: a deploy, config, data, traffic, a provider, or a timed event. Listing those changes usually cuts the search to a handful. Reading code first searches everything with no clue about where to look.
why: Code that worked all morning did not change by itself at 14:05, so reading it first has no starting point.
A restart might hide the symptom and destroys evidence such as the process state.
History is useful context, but it does not point at what started this incident.

artifact.code:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/app/relay/tools/orders.py", line 38, in lookup_order
    order = await fetch_order(int(args["order_id"]))
ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'A-8812'

The above exception was the direct cause of the following exception:

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/app/relay/agent/tools.py", line 57, in call_tool
    raise ToolError(f"{name} failed") from exc
relay.agent.tools.ToolError: lookup_order failed

quiz.q: What should the investigation focus on?
options: Why `call_tool` raises ToolError instead of returning a result
Why `fetch_order` is slow for this order
Why an order id with an `A-` prefix reached `lookup_order`
Why the traceback has two blocks instead of one
quiz.explain: The first block is the original error: the code assumed numeric order ids and received 'A-8812'. ToolError is a deliberate wrapper and is behaving as designed. The tempting move is to investigate the last line because it is what the tracker shows.
why: Wrapping the error is intended behavior; it reports the failure rather than causing it.
`fetch_order` was never called, since `int()` failed while building its argument.
Two blocks mean the code chained the errors with `from`, which is correct and helpful.

quiz.q: About 600 commits separate a known good release from the broken head. With a reliable reproduction, roughly how many test runs will `git bisect` need?
options: About 10
About 30
About 60
About 300
quiz.explain: Each step halves the range: 600, 300, 150, 75, 38, 19, 10, 5, 3, 2, 1, so about 10 steps. 300 is what a linear search would average, which is the cost bisection avoids.
why: Thirty steps would cover a range of about a billion commits.
Sixty is a tenth of the range, as if each step removed a fixed share instead of half.
Three hundred is the average for checking commits one by one.

quiz.context: About 2 percent of Relay's chat requests fail with a 500 and succeed on retry. Relay runs six API pods.

artifact.title: Failures in the last 24 hours, grouped
artifact.code:
by pod:      api-1: 0  api-2: 0  api-3: 212  api-4: 0  api-5: 0  api-6: 0
by tool:     spread across all tools
by ticket:   212 different tickets
image tag:   api-1..2,4..6: relay:v2.15   api-3: relay:v2.15

options: Add a retry for 500s in the web app
Roll back v2.15 on all pods
Profile the agent loop for slow tools
Compare api-3's effective config, node, and connections with another pod
quiz.explain: Every failure is on one pod running the same image as the others, so the code is ruled out and the difference lies in that pod's environment: its config, its node, or its connections. Rolling back the image on all pods targets code that five healthy pods also run.
why: A retry hides the failures while one pod keeps failing.
The same image runs on five pods with zero failures, so the code is cleared.
Failures spread across all tools and tickets, so no single slow path explains them.

quiz.context: Relay's help-center search returns good articles on a laptop and nothing in production. Same commit in both.

artifact.title: Effective config and one query, both environments
artifact.code:
laptop                  production
EMBED_MODEL           embed-v3                embed-v4
INDEX_BUILT_WITH      embed-v3                embed-v3
MIN_SIMILARITY        0.5                     0.5
top score for query   0.81                    0.14

quiz.q: What is the most likely cause?
options: The production index is missing articles
Queries are embedded with a different model than the index
The similarity threshold is too high in production
The production database is slower than the laptop's
quiz.explain: Production embeds queries with embed-v4 while the index holds embed-v3 vectors, and vectors from different models are not comparable, so every score is low and the threshold filters everything. The threshold looks guilty but is the same in both environments.
why: A missing article would lower some results, not drop the best score for every query to 0.14.
The threshold is 0.5 in both places; it only exposes the low scores.
Slowness changes latency, not similarity scores.

quiz.q: Intermittent `KeyError: 'shipping'` errors stop after a teammate changes `order['shipping']` to `order.get('shipping')`. Nobody knows why some orders lack the key. What is the main risk?
options: The `.get` call is slower than indexing
The change will cause a new KeyError elsewhere at once
Orders missing shipping data now flow on silently with None
The error tracker will stop recording other errors
quiz.explain: The change removed the symptom without explaining it. Orders without shipping data still exist, and now code downstream receives None and may quote wrong delivery dates without any error. The cause, why the key is missing, is still unknown.
why: The speed difference is negligible and irrelevant to correctness.
The None travels on quietly; it may surface later and far away, or never as an error.
Other errors are still recorded; only this one is hidden.

quiz.q: A refund calculation is wrong for about 1 in 500 production requests. You cannot reproduce it locally and cannot pause production processes. What is the best next step?
options: Add logging of the inputs and intermediate values, keyed by request id
Attach a debugger to a production worker and wait
Write a unit test for the refund function and see if it fails
Rewrite the calculation more carefully
quiz.explain: When a failure is rare and only in production, logging the values that matter is the way to capture it. A debugger needs a reproduction or a paused process, and a unit test needs to know which input fails, which is exactly what is missing. Once logs reveal the input, write the failing test.
why: Pausing a production worker is ruled out, and waiting for a 1-in-500 event at a breakpoint is impractical.
A test only fails if you already know the failing input, which you do not yet.
Rewriting without knowing the fault may keep the bug and add new ones.

quiz.context: Release v2.16 went out at 10:00 with an additive migration (a new nullable column) and new refund code. Since 10:02, 30 percent of refunds fail. The cause is not yet understood.
options: Ship a hotfix based on the most likely theory
Roll back both the code and the migration
Keep investigating, since 70 percent of refunds still work
Roll back the code, leave the column, then investigate
quiz.explain: The failures started two minutes after the deploy, the cause is unknown, and the old code ignores an added nullable column, so rolling back the code is safe and stops the damage. Reversing the migration drops data written since 10:00 for no gain. A hotfix on a theory risks a second bug.
why: A fix based on an unconfirmed theory can fail or add a new bug while customers keep failing.
Dropping the new column destroys data, and old code does not need it removed.
Thirty percent of refunds failing is ongoing customer harm that a safe rollback stops.

quiz.q: Relay's ticket summarizer works on your laptop and fails in production. Which of these are cheap moves that split the search space? Select all that apply.
options: Replay the exact failing production input on your laptop
Diff the effective environment variables in both places
Compare installed package versions in both places
Restart the production pods to clear their state
Rewrite the summarizer to be more defensive
quiz.explain: Each of the first three tests one class of difference, data, config, or dependencies, and costs minutes. A restart destroys evidence and tests nothing, and a defensive rewrite is a fix applied before the cause is known.

quiz.q: Put the steps of the debugging loop in order.
items: State expected and actual behavior, scope, and start time
List what changed around the start time
Rank hypotheses and write a prediction for the top one
Run one experiment that changes or measures one thing
Record the result and what it rules out
Confirm the cause explains every observation before closing
quiz.explain: A precise statement and the change list come first because they shrink the field before any experiment. Recording comes after each test so ruled-out ideas stay ruled out, and the last check guards against a fix that only hid the symptom.

quiz.q: Match each statement to the trap it shows.
pairs: 'Here is a cache miss, so it must be the cache'
'I added a retry and the errors are gone'
'It broke after my deploy, revert it' (failures began earlier)
'The log says the flag is off' (yesterday's log)
'NoneType has no attribute' in the formatter
quiz.explain: Each trap replaces evidence with a feeling of progress. The counters are the same: predict what you would see if you were wrong, check timing and scope, and verify where each piece of evidence came from.

quiz.context: A new version of Relay's system prompt contains eight separate edits. On the nightly eval its pass rate is 74 percent against 83 percent for the old prompt. Run-to-run variation on this eval is about 2 points.
quiz.q: How would you find which edit caused the drop?
rubric: Checks first that errored or infrastructure failures are not inflating the drop
Holds the model, dataset, and settings fixed across runs
Bisects the edits: apply half, rerun, keep the half that carries the drop
Accounts for noise, by repeating runs or requiring a gap well above 2 points
Notes that edits may interact, so the culprit may be a pair
quiz.model: First confirm the drop is in graded answers, not errors. Then hold the model, dataset, and settings fixed and bisect: apply four edits to the old prompt and rerun. A drop near 9 points means the culprit is in those four; near zero means the other four. Halve again, about three rounds. Repeat runs when results land near the 2-point noise, and if no single edit reproduces the drop, test pairs, since edits can interact.

drills.title: The order lookup that broke after the deploy
drills.brief: Since Monday morning, about 6 percent of Relay chats end with 'I could not find your order.' The error tracker shows a spike of `ToolError: lookup_order failed`. Release v2.14 shipped Monday at 10:30 with 40 commits. A teammate says 'it's obviously v2.14, let's roll back'.

artifact.title: Error tracker summary
artifact.code:
ToolError: lookup_order failed
first seen:  Mon 09:14     events: 1,906     users: 1,402
releases:    v2.13 (212 events), v2.14 (1,694 events)

steps.q: What do you look at first?
options: The full chained traceback of one failed event
The diff of all 40 commits in v2.14
The LLM provider's status page
Postgres CPU and connection graphs
steps.explain: The wrapper error says only that the tool failed. One full traceback, already stored, shows the original error and the line, which splits code, data, and infrastructure in one read. Reading 40 commits searches the whole release before you know what to look for.
steps.reveal: The first block shows `ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'A-8812'` at `orders.py` line 38. Other events show 'A-9020', 'A-9133'.

artifact.code:
File "/app/relay/tools/orders.py", line 38, in lookup_order
    order = await fetch_order(int(args["order_id"]))
ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'A-8812'

The above exception was the direct cause of the following exception:
...

steps.q: The deploy is still the obvious suspect. Which cheap check tells you whether v2.14 is to blame?
options: Roll back v2.14 and watch the error rate for an hour
Check when line 38 last changed and when the first `A-` order was created
Ask the model to stop sending order ids with prefixes
Rerun the nightly eval against v2.13 and v2.14
steps.explain: Two lookups answer it: if line 38 predates v2.14, the code did not change, and the first `A-` order's creation time shows when the new input appeared. The summary already hinted at this, since the error was first seen at 09:14 under v2.13. A rollback takes an hour and changes production to learn the same thing.
steps.reveal: Line 38 has not changed in eight months. The first order with an `A-` id was created at 09:12 on Monday, when the business launched a marketplace sales channel. Its orders use prefixed ids. v2.14 is innocent; it simply received most of the traffic.

options: Catch the ValueError and tell the model the order was not found
Strip the `A-` prefix before converting the id to an integer
Treat order ids as strings end to end and add a test with an `A-` id
Roll back v2.14 until the marketplace team changes its id format
steps.explain: Order ids are no longer numbers, so the code's assumption is what broke. Catching the error tells customers their real orders do not exist. Stripping the prefix may fetch a different order with the same number. Rolling back changes nothing, since v2.13 has the same line.
steps.reveal: The tool schema, the parser, and the query now treat `order_id` as a string, and a test covers both id formats.

steps.q: How do you confirm the fix explains the whole incident?
options: Watch the error tracker for an hour after deploying
Ask a few marketplace customers to try again
Replay Monday's failed tool calls against the fix and check failures by sales channel
Run the existing nightly eval and compare the pass rate
steps.explain: Replaying the captured failing inputs proves the fix handles exactly the cases that failed, and splitting by channel checks that marketplace orders account for all of them. The existing eval has no `A-` orders, so it cannot show anything about this bug.
steps.reveal: All 1,906 failed calls succeed on replay, and every one of them was a marketplace order. The team adds recent marketplace tickets to the eval set.

drills.debrief: Root cause: a new sales channel introduced string order ids, and `lookup_order` had always assumed integers. The deploy at 10:30 was a coincidence that the error tracker's grouping by release made look guilty. Reading the chained traceback and checking the first-seen time cleared it in minutes. The fix treats ids as strings everywhere and adds both formats to tests and evals. The general lesson: check timing and scope before blaming the newest change.

drills.title: One message in fifty disappears
drills.brief: About 2 percent of customer messages fail with 'Something went wrong, please try again', and sending again works. The rate was below 0.5 percent until last week. Last week the team upgraded the Postgres driver and shipped a new mobile layout for the chat screen. A teammate wants to add an automatic retry and move on.

artifact.title: 500s on POST /tickets/{id}/messages, daily
artifact.code:
Mon 0.4%   Tue 0.3%   Wed 0.4%   <- driver upgrade Wed 18:00
Thu 0.4%   Fri 2.1%   <- mobile layout Fri 09:00
Sat 2.3%   Sun 1.9%

options: Add an automatic retry on 500 in the web and mobile apps
Roll back the Postgres driver upgrade
Group the failed requests by their error text and by what else was happening on that ticket
Scale up Postgres in case it is overloaded
steps.explain: The daily rates already clear the driver: Thursday stayed at 0.4 percent after Wednesday's upgrade, and the jump came Friday with the mobile layout. Grouping the failures' errors costs minutes and says what kind of fault it is. A retry would hide it and could send a customer's message twice.
steps.reveal: All failures share one error. Every failed request inserts a message into a ticket.

artifact.code:
ERROR:  duplicate key value violates unique constraint "messages_ticket_id_seq_key"
DETAIL:  Key (ticket_id, seq)=(451, 7) already exists.

steps.q: A duplicate `(ticket_id, seq)` means two inserts chose the same sequence number. What do you compare next?
options: Whether each failure had another message for the same ticket within a second
Failure rates by hour of day
Failure rates by API pod
The driver's changelog for unique constraint changes
steps.explain: Two writers picking the same number suggests two requests for the same ticket at the same moment. Checking for a neighbor request on the same ticket tests that directly. Pods and hours are reasonable groupings in general, but the error already points at per-ticket concurrency.
steps.reveal: Every failure had a second POST for the same ticket within 300 ms. Most came from the new mobile layout, where the send button is easy to tap twice.

steps.q: How do you confirm the mechanism before fixing it?
options: Wait for a week of production data under the current layout
Send pairs of concurrent messages to one ticket in staging and count failures
Read the message insert code and reason about it
Roll back the mobile layout and watch the rate
steps.explain: A targeted replay raises the failure rate from 2 percent to something you can measure in a minute, and compares it with a control. Reading the code is a good companion, but only an experiment confirms that this race is the one in production. Rolling back the layout would reduce double taps without proving the mechanism.
steps.reveal: Concurrent pairs on one ticket fail 31 times in 100; pairs on different tickets and sequential sends never fail. The insert computes `max(seq) + 1` and then writes it, with nothing stopping two requests from reading the same max.

options: Disable the send button for one second after each tap
Catch the duplicate key error and return 200
Retry the whole request from the app on any 500
Assign the sequence atomically in Postgres, and dedupe sends by a client message id
steps.explain: The race is in the write, so it must be fixed there: lock the ticket row or let the database assign the number. A double tap would then create two identical messages, so a client-generated message id used as an idempotency key removes those. Disabling the button only shrinks the race, and returning 200 loses the message.
steps.reveal: With both changes, concurrent pairs succeed in staging and duplicates are merged. Production 500s on this endpoint fall below 0.05 percent.

drills.debrief: Root cause: message numbering used read-then-write with no lock, a race that had always been there at a low rate. The new mobile layout made double taps common and raised the rate fourfold. The driver upgrade was the obvious suspect and the daily numbers cleared it for free. Fixes: atomic sequence assignment and a client message id. A concurrency test on the insert would have caught it early. The general lesson: an intermittent failure has a condition; find it and raise its rate.
